summary:
Colorado stands under the United States federal framework, which sets the baseline a trans visitor carries into the state: since January 2025 federal identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth, the X marker is no longer issued, airport screening follows national procedures that can disclose a traveller's trans status, and visa discretion over transgender athletes seeking entry for women's sporting events applies at any port of entry including Denver. State law here runs against that current rather than with it.

The Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act expressly covers gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing and public accommodations, and the legislature expanded that coverage again in 2025. Public-accommodation coverage is the provision a visitor would rely on directly, in hotels, restaurants, shops and venues.

Colorado's highest court has enforced that protection against federal pressure. On 18 May 2026 the Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated state anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Justice William Hood wrote that continuing treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision denied the petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity; two justices dissented on the ground that federal threats could shut the hospital system.

The limits of that protection are visible in funding. From 13 October 2026 Colorado suspends Medicaid coverage of hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth because a federal rule finalised in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care under age 18, and under 19 in the CHP+ child programme; the state Medicaid agency says resuming coverage will require legislative action. State protections here are therefore operative but exposed to national defunding.

Detention risk should be assessed on the same terms. Colorado has no identity-based housing statute for prisons. Transgender women were historically held in men's facilities in the state system, and the relief achieved came through litigation rather than a baseline rule: a 2019 class action alleging sexual and physical violence and denial of care produced a court-approved 2024 consent decree, Raven v. Polis, in Denver District Court requiring expanded health care, voluntary specialised housing and payments of about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admission of liability. An earlier 2019 settlement paid Lindsay Saunders-Velez $170,000 over the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison.
tangentialFactors:
A national legal risk assessment dated July 2026 lists Colorado among the most protective states for transgender people, alongside California, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota and New Jersey, and counts the state among those with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage. The same assessment period produced do-not-travel designations elsewhere in the country, so the contrast between this state and four flagged states shapes any multi-state itinerary.

The direction of travel is contested rather than settled. Conservative activists have qualified three measures for the November 2026 Colorado ballot, two of which would write restrictions on transgender minors into state law, so the protective framework described above will be voted on while a visitor is present or shortly afterward.

The Medicaid suspension shows Colorado's own guarantees operating under direct federal-funding pressure, a pattern that also produced the hospital's voluntary suspension of care and the two-justice dissent in the May 2026 ruling. Federal document, screening and visa rules remain the dominant exposure at the border regardless of state law.
localsOnly:
Colorado voters decide on 3 November 2026 whether to ban transgender children from gendered sports that do not align with their biological sex (Initiative 109) and whether to prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering their sex characteristics (Initiative 110), after state elections officials certified voter signatures on three measures including Initiative 108 on child sex trafficking. If certified measures pass, restrictions on transgender minors enter state statute.

Medicaid coverage of hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth ends 13 October 2026 under the August 2026 federal rule; about 500 youth under 19 received Medicaid-covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25. Patients already taking hormones keep coverage through a six-month tapering period, and behavioural healthcare is unaffected. Resuming coverage will require legislative action, according to the state Medicaid agency.

Residents hold anti-discrimination protection in employment, housing and public accommodations under CADA, with gender identity and gender expression expressly included and coverage expanded again in 2025. The Colorado Supreme Court's 18 May 2026 order requires Children's Hospital Colorado to resume gender-affirming care for transgender youth, including puberty blockers and hormone therapy.

Prison placement for transgender people in state custody is governed by the 2024 consent decree in Raven v. Polis rather than by statute: the decree requires the Colorado Department of Corrections to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing comprising a 100-bed unit at the men's Sterling facility and an integration unit at the women's prison, and pay roughly $2.1 million to about 400 class members without admitting liability. The 2019 Lindsay Saunders-Velez settlement paid $170,000 over the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the injunction ordering the hospital to resume care survives further federal or appellate challenge is unresolved in the available material; the two-justice dissent recorded the argument that federal threats could shut the hospital system.

Whether Colorado issues driver's licences or birth certificates bearing a gender marker other than sex assigned at birth, and what a Colorado-issued identifier does at federal screening, is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved.

The enforcement record of CADA public-accommodation claims brought by out-of-state visitors, as distinct from residents, is not sourced here.

Whether the November 2026 ballot measures will pass, and their effect on facilities, sports and minors' care if they do, is pending and not sourced beyond certification of the signatures.

Whether the consent decree's voluntary specialised housing is available to a non-resident held in state custody, and the conditions of any transfer request, are not addressed in the available material.
